description: Hi, my name is Leo, and I'm a freshman at Ballantyne Ridge High School. I like to code and analyze data, so this is a very fun opportunity for me. I am looking for people with some coding experience and interest in space. That's all you need. I'm just here to have fun.
summary: Astronuggets is a game you play in your browser where you run a Mars base in Jezero Crater for 20 sols. You split a small solar power supply between five buildings: the habitat, solar array, food silo, research lab, and comms dish. You also have to keep the radiation shield up and earn 80 science points. You can walk around the 3D base in first person, flip switches, spend scrap on upgrades, and deal with a new emergency every night. The hard part is that power never stretches far enough. Run the lab and life support suffers. Skip maintenance and things break. Each night’s choices have hidden odds and no labels telling you which one is safe, so you have to think it through and take a risk. The solar flares and dust storms come from real NASA data, so you learn to plan a day ahead. Kids 9 and up get the full game. Younger kids get Mars Base Jr., which is simpler and slower. We think it matters because kids don’t just hear that space missions are about trade-offs. They feel it when their base runs out of power. This helps kids truly understand the feeling of running a space base.
details:
What it does:

AstroNuggets is a browser game where you run a Mars base in Jezero Crater for 20 sols. You share a small solar power supply between five buildings: habitat, solar array, food silo, research lab, and comms dish. You also keep the radiation shield up and try to reach 80 science points. You can walk around the 3D base in first person. Every night something goes wrong and you pick one of four choices. They aren't labeled and the odds are hidden, so you have to think about the risk yourself.

Kids 9 and up play the full game. Younger kids play Mars Base Jr., which is simpler and slower. An age question at the start decides which one they get.

Benefits and impact:

Kids see that running a space mission is about trade-offs. If you power the lab, life support might run short. If you skip maintenance, something breaks later. It runs in any browser with nothing to install, so a teacher can use it in class right away.

Tools:

It's one HTML file made with JavaScript and Three.js. The storm and flare schedules are based on real NASA data (DONKI and Curiosity RAD). We built it with Claude Code and tested it with Node and Playwright scripts. The trailer was made with ffmpeg.

What's creative:

Most kids' games tell you which answer is right. Here nothing tells you, so kids have to weigh risk on their own. We also made two versions so younger kids can learn the same ideas without being overwhelmed.

What we considered:

We thought about difficulty for different ages, using real NASA data, keeping the game from being too easy, and making sure stat changes are clear on screen. We also fixed glitches and tested the whole game before finishing.
